recent.narrative: Extreme Drought in Jim Hogg County expanded markedly by December 23, with approximately 75% of the County under this condition, up from around 25% beforehand in December.  Far western and the southeast corner of the county remained at Severe (D2), based on small pockets of rain during mid December.

Severe (D2) Drought would prevail across the western and southern portions of Jim Hogg County, with an area of Extreme (D3) Drought across northeastern portions of the County, to the edge of Hebbronville, through the 22nd.

Extreme (D3) Drought developed across the eastern third of Jim Hogg County, including Hebbronville and ranches along and south of State Highway 285, on November 18th and continued through and beyond month's end.  The combination of dryness, warm to hot temperatures, and very low soil moisture contributed to the worsening condition.  Severe (D2) Drought continued elsewhere in the county.

Due to prolonged dryness, Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across all of Jim Hogg County that included Hebbronville. Drought conditions persisted through the remainder of the month for all but the northeast corner, where Extreme (D3) conditions would develop on the 18th.

Following locally heavy rainfall before daybreak on May 7th, and again during the afternoon no May 8th, which dropped pockets of 2-4+ inches of rain across much of Zapata and western/southern Jim Hogg County, Drought Improved to Moderate (D1) and Abnormally Dry (D0) across all but the northern quarter of the County, including Hebbronville, for the May 13th Drought Monitor.  This area received much less rainfall - around 0.5 inches - insufficient for improvement there.  Limited rainfall for the remainder of May allowed D2 conditions to hold in northern Jim Hogg.

Due to the continued combination of dry and hot conditions with a strong sun angle and evaporation rates, Severe (D2) Drought continued across northern and western Jim Hogg County to begin May.  A band of thunderstorms with 1 to 2 inches (estimated) of rain on May 2nd covered extreme southwest Jim Hogg County, reducing the drought coverage to the remove that sliver for the May 6th monitor.

costliest.narrative: A large tornado began near Hwy 1130, flipping a double wide mobile home that was tied down. A woman inside was critically injured. Other homes along Hwy 1130 had trees fall on them, roofs ripped off, and wind blown debris damage. The tornado continued north on South Teal Road, blowing down trees. Along Hudnall Road, several homes and garages lost their roofs. The tornado turned a little to the northeast, and hit the Woodland Ridge Acres subdivision off of Hwy 87, blowing down more trees. Max estimated wind speed was 130 MPH. The tornado continued into Newton County.

A tornado touched down south of Old Hwy 90 near the Hwy 62 exit on I-10, severely damaging a brick home. A large building in the backyard was destroyed, an RV was tossed 25 yards, a truck flipped over, and 3 other vehicles were pushed out of the driveway. An ATV stored in the building in the backyard was picked up by the tornado and tossed across I-10. Further to the north on Hwy 62 at the TX DOT office, large warehouses in the back had the overhead doors blown in. Max estimated winds were 130 MPH.

The Orange-Calcasieu Tornado touched down near Orangefield Road and quickly produced EF-2 damage a few blocks northwest of Orangefield High School. This area sustained the most severe damage from this tornado, where winds were estimated to max out at 120 mph. Numerous homes were either heavily damaged or destroyed. The tornado then crossed over Cow Bayou, and produced mostly EF-1 damage through the rest of Orange County.  The tornado crossed the Sabine River over a section of West Bluff Road. costliest.narrative: This is segment #2 of 4 of a multi-segmented EF-3 supercellular tornado that began in Montague County, crossed into Cooke County, Denton County, and then back into Cooke County. The tornado was ongoing for about an hour and a half with a total path length just under 48 miles. The tornado was the strongest in Cooke County and resulted in 7 fatalities in Cooke County. ||The tornado entered Cooke County at 1008 pm CDT time and exited into Denton County at 1049 pm CDT for a total path length of 25.41 miles. The tornado path zigzagged at times. The maximum width of the damage path is measured at over a mile in the area west of Valley View; however this is misleading. We do not believe the tornado was over a mile wide, but instead there were a few smaller circulations rotating around the main tornado circulation which was likely a maximum width of about 1200 yards (.68 miles wide). A lingering upper trough provided several days of thunderstorm activity across the region, with a dryline providing focus for development each day from Thursday May 4 through Monday May 8. Several of these storms were severe with damaging winds and large hail.

Multiple rounds of thunderstorms occurred from Monday April 8 through Wednesday April 10 as a deep low pressure system moved east through the Rockies, eventually transitioning to an open trough as it traversed the Plains. The first round of thunderstorms began immediately after the region experienced a total solar eclipse! Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence on April 8th, though flooding became a primary issue on the 9th and 10th following several rounds of showers and storms.
A large 5th wheel was tipped over onto a truck parked next to it, and a small wood shed on the same property was blown across the field.

A second consecutive day of severe thunderstorms affected the South Plains and Rolling Plains of West Texas but saw increased coverage on the sixth. Strong moisture was still in place across the area and with increasing surface heating, ample instability was available for explosive supercell thunderstorm development. A lingering thunderstorm outflow boundary, from early morning convection in the Texas Panhandle, sagged southward through the day. Thunderstorms initially developed along this feature across the central South Plains and quickly became severe. The scattered nature of convective initiation allowed some areas to see repeated rounds of severe thunderstorms. One supercell thunderstorm that tracked across Hockley County produced at least three known tornadoes. However, these tornadoes only briefly touched down causing no known damage. A slow moving upper level low emerged from New Mexico and passed slowly across the South Plains region on the eighth. On the night of the seventh, a cold front moved through the region lowering temperatures for snow production. Initially, the air moving in behind the cold front was lacking in low level moisture. However, moisture gradually increased throughout the day as lift persisted ahead of the approaching upper level low. This led to precipitation expanding in coverage and intensify over the extreme southern Texas Panhandle and northern Rolling Plains during the afternoon and evening. Wind speeds quickly rose after sunrise immediately in advance of a band of precipitation racing southeastward from the western Texas Panhandle into the northern and central South Plains. A large slow-moving trough across the Four Corners combined with very rich low-level moisture to produce widespread severe weather and localized flash flooding, especially across portions of southeast New Mexico and west Texas.

recent.narrative: A large but strong upper level ridge of high pressure expanded from the Southern Rockies/Central and Southern Plains into the Mid-Mississippi Valley on August 14th, with compressional warming beneath the ridge contributing to extensive warming across much of Southwest Arkansas, Southeast Oklahoma, and East Texas. Sinking air beneath the ridge and strong insolation allowed for afternoon temperatures to climb into the upper 90s to near 100 degrees over these areas. When combined with the high humidity, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees across much of Southwest Arkansas, Southeast Oklahoma, and East Texas, which persisted through the 20th.

An upper level ridge of high pressure was centered over much of Texas on August 8th-9th, with increased subsidence beneath the ridge allowing temperatures across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, extreme Southwest Arkansas, and Northwest Louisiana to climb into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees. A light southerly wind on the backside of surface high pressure over the Lower Mississippi Valley maintained ample low level moisture and limited the extent of mixing, resulting in heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees across the aforementioned areas.

A weak cool front began to sink south into Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas during the day on August 1st, ahead of an upper level trough of low pressure that shifted southeast through the region. Compressional warming ahead of the front resulted in temperatures climbing into the mid and upper 90s across Lower East Texas and North Louisiana along and south of Interstate 20. Low level moisture pooling along the frontal zone did not allow for much mixing of the dewpoints during the afternoon, which when combined with these temperatures, resulted in heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees.

An upper level ridge of high pressure over the Southeast United States began to retrograde west across the Lower Mississippi Valley into the Four State Region during the final several days of July, resulting in the return of much hotter temperatures as they climbed back into the mid 90s to near 100 degrees. While dewpoints were able to mix out to some extent, resultant heat indices still ranged from 105 to 110 degrees from the 27th through the 31st across much of East Texas before showers and thunderstorms that developed during the afternoon of the 31st significantly cooled temperatures late in the day.

Following the passage of a westward moving tropical wave on July 19th across North Louisiana and East Texas, upper ridging expanded back west into much of the Four State Region from the Southeast Gulf Coast on the 20th, and persisted through the 25th. Strong subsidence beneath the ridge resulted in additional compressional warming, which enabled afternoon temperatures to climb into the mid and upper 90s across Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, extreme Eastern Texas and North Louisiana. Coupled with ample low level moisture that persisted across the area, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees each day.

Upper ridging expanded west from the Southeast Gulf Coast into much of the Four State Region from July 15th-17th. Strong subsidence beneath the ridge resulted in compressional warming, which enabled afternoon temperatures each day to climb into the mid and upper 90s across North Louisiana, extreme Southern Arkansas and Eastern Texas. Coupled with ample low level moisture that persisted across the area, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees each day.

Montague County received the majority of the severe weather, as the triple point between the dryline, cold front, and warm front remained stationary near that location for several hours. Storms eventually expanded south, and spread east through the rest of the region late that afternoon and into the evening. Hail up to 4.5 inches was reported in the Saint Jo area in Montague County. In addition, 3 brief tornadoes occurred in counties along the Red River: 1 EF-Unknown, and 2 EF-0s.

A strong upper-level high pressure ridge expanded and intensified across the South Central and Southeast portions of the U.S. late in the month of June and persisted for several days. Increasing southerly flow in response to the eastward advancing high pressure ridge allowed rich Gulf moisture and elevated humidity levels to combine with daily high temperatures in the lower to middle 90s across all of East and Northeast Texas, resulting in peak heat index values between 105-109 degrees each day from June 20th through June 24th.

A large but strong upper level ridge of high pressure expanded from the Southern Rockies/Central and Southern Plains into the Mid-Mississippi Valley on August 14th, with compressional warming beneath the ridge contributing to extensive warming across much of Southwest Arkansas, Southeast Oklahoma, and East Texas. Sinking air beneath the ridge and strong insolation allowed for afternoon temperatures to climb into the upper 90s to near 100 degrees over these areas. When combined with the high humidity, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees across much of Southwest Arkansas, Southeast Oklahoma, and East Texas, which persisted through the 20th.

An upper level ridge of high pressure was centered over much of Texas on August 8th-9th, with increased subsidence beneath the ridge allowing temperatures across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, extreme Southwest Arkansas, and Northwest Louisiana to climb into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees. A light southerly wind on the backside of surface high pressure over the Lower Mississippi Valley maintained ample low level moisture and limited the extent of mixing, resulting in heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees across the aforementioned areas.

A weak cool front began to sink south into Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas during the day on August 1st, ahead of an upper level trough of low pressure that shifted southeast through the region. Compressional warming ahead of the front resulted in temperatures climbing into the mid and upper 90s across Lower East Texas and North Louisiana along and south of Interstate 20. Low level moisture pooling along the frontal zone did not allow for much mixing of the dewpoints during the afternoon, which when combined with these temperatures, resulted in heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees.

An upper level ridge of high pressure over the Southeast United States began to retrograde west across the Lower Mississippi Valley into the Four State Region during the final several days of July, resulting in the return of much hotter temperatures as they climbed back into the mid 90s to near 100 degrees. While dewpoints were able to mix out to some extent, resultant heat indices still ranged from 105 to 110 degrees from the 27th through the 31st across much of East Texas before showers and thunderstorms that developed during the afternoon of the 31st significantly cooled temperatures late in the day.

Following the passage of a westward moving tropical wave on July 19th across North Louisiana and East Texas, upper ridging expanded back west into much of the Four State Region from the Southeast Gulf Coast on the 20th, and persisted through the 25th. Strong subsidence beneath the ridge resulted in additional compressional warming, which enabled afternoon temperatures to climb into the mid and upper 90s across Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, extreme Eastern Texas and North Louisiana. Coupled with ample low level moisture that persisted across the area, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees each day.

Upper ridging expanded west from the Southeast Gulf Coast into much of the Four State Region from July 15th-17th. Strong subsidence beneath the ridge resulted in compressional warming, which enabled afternoon temperatures each day to climb into the mid and upper 90s across North Louisiana, extreme Southern Arkansas and Eastern Texas. Coupled with ample low level moisture that persisted across the area, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees each day.

A tornado formed just northwest of Navarro Mills Lake, just east of the Navarro/Hill County line. Damage near this initiation point was confined to split tree trunks consistent with EF-0 intensity windspeeds. The tornado tracked east-northeastward, causing tree damage and impacting multiple residences and outbuildings in areas between FM 744 and Navarro Mills Lake. Most of this damage was EF-0 to low end EF-1 in character, consistent with windspeeds of 75-95 mph. Damage was mainly associated with roof and fascia damage on the residences and significant sheet metal damage on outbuildings. However, one manufactured home was totally destroyed on Navarro County Road 3091, consistent with EF-1 winds estimated at around 110 mph. The tornado crossed FM 744, and dissipated just northwest of the Dresden community.

A tornado formed approximately 2 miles southwest of Barry in open country, based on storm spotter video and eyewitness reports. This tornado moved north and northeast of Barry, impacting several residences and outbuildings along Navarro County roads 1210 and 1230. Most of the structural damage was confined to roofs and outbuilding sheet metal and was consistent with damage intensities of EF-0 and lower end EF-1 magnitude. However, one manufactured home along CR 1230 was totally destroyed, consistent with EF-1 winds of approximately 110 mph. The tornado traveled several additional miles to the east, passing north of Emhouse and producing EF-0 damage to trees and outbuildings. This tornado eventually dissipated in the Chambers Creek drainage west of Rice.

A brief EF-0 tornado occurred west of Frost in far northwestern Navarro County. A grain elevator was impacted and partially collapsed along State Highway 22 west of Frost. The tornado crossed the highway and produced some EF-0 roof and garage door damage to several homes on the west side of Frost. The tornado dissipated just north of Frost. Maximum estimated winds were 80 mph.

Precipitation rates increased overnight, becoming predominantly snow during the early morning hours of the 21st, then diminished during the late morning. One NWS employee measured 0.1875 inches of an ice and sleet mixture accumulated on their personal snow table early in the morning. Later reports from the public, CoCoRaHS station TX-GV-76, a HAM radio operator, a trained storm spotter and multiple NWS employees showed 1.75-3.2 inches of snowfall across the area. The highest amounts were measured around Dickinson and League City.
Texas Department of Transportation reported water on Texas highway 87 where it meets State highway 124.
Bay Harbor area of Galveston had 16 to 18 inches of coastal flooding.
A 17-year-old from Louisiana drowned on west side of Tower 25 according to Beach Patrol.
Widespread coastal flooding was reported around the city of Clear Lake Shores.

A second consecutive day of severe thunderstorms affected the South Plains and Rolling Plains of West Texas but saw increased coverage on the sixth. Strong moisture was still in place across the area and with increasing surface heating, ample instability was available for explosive supercell thunderstorm development. A lingering thunderstorm outflow boundary, from early morning convection in the Texas Panhandle, sagged southward through the day. Thunderstorms initially developed along this feature across the central South Plains and quickly became severe. The scattered nature of convective initiation allowed some areas to see repeated rounds of severe thunderstorms. One supercell thunderstorm that tracked across Hockley County produced at least three known tornadoes. However, these tornadoes only briefly touched down causing no known damage. Thunderstorms initially developed over the southeastern Texas Panhandle early in the afternoon and quickly moved east into southwestern Oklahoma. A much strong complex of supercell thunderstorms moved southeastward out of the central Texas Panhandle creating widespread damaging wind gusts and very large hail. Numerous roads were closed or impassable in Hall and Childress Counties including US Highway 287 between Memphis and Estelline and Texas State Highway 256 between Memphis and Lakeview. One vehicle accident was reported on Texas State Highway 86 northeast of Turkey. The Prairie Dog Town Fork of the Red River filled its banks between Estelline and Childress briefly reaching minor flood stage at the Childress 10N river gage.

Both Childress municipal airport and the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Childress measured severe wind gusts spanning from 2256 CST through 2316 CST. A peak wind gust of 64 was measured at 2313 CST and 2316 CST.

The Automated Surface Observing System at Childress Municipal Airport measured a severe wind gust to 65 mph.

Showers and thunderstorms developed in an unstable airmass during the late afternoon of August 11th. Storms mainly developed across the I-40 corridor and shifted south through the evening hours. These storms quickly grew to be severe and produce large hail thanks to colder temperatures in the upper atmosphere. A few storms produced gusty winds and localized wind damage. Efficient rainfall led to high rainfall rates and some localized flash flooding.

Half dollar size hail fell about three miles east of Wellington. Numerous tree limbs were also blown down due to wind. However, the hail was more destructive about a mile to the southeast where a cotton field was completely destroyed.

Several scattered storms developed and intensified across central and eastern portions of the Panhandles during the evening of July 8th. Relatively strong wind shear and instability allowed storms to become severe and bring hail up to half dollar size and 60mph winds to portions of the eastern combined Panhandles, which resulted in crop damage. Additional storms developed along outflow boundaries as they moved across the central Texas Panhandle. These additional storms produced severe wind and hail.
This 62mph wind gust was observed from a decaying thunderstorm at the Dozier mesonet.

Scattered showers and thunderstorms moved across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles starting late on the 2nd and continuing through the evening of the 3rd. First storms moved from the southeast to northwest, changing over to move west to east motion and finally with the final wave, they moved from the north-northwest to south-southeast. On the evening of the 2nd a couple of isolated storm became severe producing winds up to 70 to 80 mph over Randall and Collingsworth Counties. Then on the evening of the 3rd additional thunderstorms became severe through wind gusts reaching up to 60 to 63 mph in the TX Panhandle and the OK Panhandle.

A wet pattern set up over the Panhandles May 29 through the 31st. Instability in the atmosphere helped to create strong to severe thunderstorms first in the form of discrete cells the night of the 29th into the early AM hours of the 30th. One of which produced a tornado in the western Oklahoma Panhandle. Then subsequent nights disturbances aloft helped create a Mesoscale Convective Complex both on the night of the 30th and again on the 31st. Besides the tornado reported on the 29th this storm in Cimarron County also produced hail up to 1.75��� in diameter. On the next two nights the severe wind gusts reaching upwards of 74 mph. Severe hail was more isolated compared to the winds that were more widespread with lines of storms surging from the northwest to the southeast on the 30th and from the west-northwest to east-southeast on the night of the 31st.

During the late afternoon and early evening of July 23rd, thunderstorms formed over the northeastern Texas Panhandle into the far eastern Oklahoma Panhandle. As these storms moved east to northeast the atmosphere supported strong thunderstorms that could produced severe wind gusts. Some of these thunderstorms produced wind damage that could have resulted from winds up to 80mph.
Miami mesonet began having severe level wind gusts at 119 AM CDT with a peak gust of 90 mph. Severe gusts ended at 130 AM.

During the early afternoon of June 2nd, scattered storms developed over parts of eastern New Mexico and the far southwestern Texas Panhandle. These storms quickly grew in coverage expanding northward into a line before moving easterly across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. Some of these storms were severe with the main impact being damaging wind gusts.

In the late afternoon to early evening hours of May 18, a strong upper level storm system and surface dryline created favorable conditions for severe thunderstorms across the far eastern Panhandles. This environment was characterized by extreme instability and very high surface dewpoints in the low 70s east of the dryline, which supported all hazards of severe weather. Two supercells developed in the eastern Texas Panhandle. One moved to the north and produced large hail up to golfball size before moving into the Oklahoma Panhandle. The other also produced large hail up to baseball size along with a couple of tornadoes near the state line with western Oklahoma.
Baseball size hail occurred around 12 miles south of Higgins.

As it crossed Highway 277, it brought down about 7 power poles, and caused more impressive tree damage, snapping branches and some trees while uprooting other hardwood trees. It resulted in some minor roof damage to a shed and damaged another shed at a natural gas facility. The tornado then crossed County Road 22, just to the south of Highway 277. A more organized storm over Lipscomb County eventually emerged and went on to generate a 78 mph wind gust at the Lipscomb mesonet observation site west of town.

The overall environment was highly conducive for severe storm development, with hail as large as 3 to 3.5 inches in diameter being measured across portions of the eastern Panhandles. Due to the low level winds increasing after sunset, this allowed storms to have low level rotation which led to an increased threat for tornadoes throughout the rest of the evening. The severe thunderstorms tracked south across the eastern Texas Panhandle and Beaver county in the Oklahoma Panhandle and produced large to destructive hail and at least one known tornado. These storms were slow moving and also produced heavy rainfall that likely led to flash flooding, especially southeast of Perryton where multiple storms formed and tracked over the same location. An upper level weather disturbance moved across the region late in the evening on August 2nd through the early morning hours of August 3rd. This, combined with sufficient instability and wind shear, brought severe thunderstorms to the combined Panhandles. These storms moved in from Kansas and brought hail and damaging winds to the region. The most significant of the severe storms moved through portions of the north central Texas Panhandle, where radar estimates and associated damage from straight line winds were estimated to have reached 90 to 100mph in portions of Moore and Hutchinson counties.

Large hail fell northwest of Higgins. Hail sizes were mostly dime size to quarter size, but a few hailstones were slightly larger than a golf ball. This resulted in damage to a fire engine that was en route to a wildfire caused by lightning.

A supercell thunderstorm moved across the eastern part of Lipscomb County. It produced hail up to the size of golfballs from roughly seven miles southeast of Lipscomb to Higgins. Quarter size hail fell about seven miles to the northeast of Glazier.

Thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front on the afternoon of June 8th and rapidly became severe. costliest.narrative: Extreme cold gripped the county for several days. Overnight lows were near or below 15 degrees Fahrenheit almost all week. The period of February 15-16th was the coldest with low temperatures in the single digits to -8 degrees Fahrenheit. The maximum temperature on the 15th was only around 10 degrees Fahrenheit. Wind chill values during the 14th-16th were between 0 to -20 degrees Fahrenheit most of the time. The cold temperatures resulted in an extreme amount of damage to pipes, infrastructure, and power. According to the DSO at the time of this publication, over 6500 residences and business were affected or damaged with varying degrees of damage.

recent.narrative: A large but strong upper level ridge of high pressure that had been prevalent since mid-August persisted over the Southern Plains and Lower Mississippi Valley through the 20th,  with compressional warming beneath the ridge contributing to continued warming across Southern Arkansas, North Louisiana, and extreme Eastern Texas. Sinking air beneath the ridge and strong insolation again allowed for afternoon temperatures to climb into the upper 90s to near 100 degrees over these areas. When combined with the high humidity, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees across much of Southwest Arkansas, North Louisiana, and extreme Eastern Texas.

A large but strong upper level ridge of high pressure expanded from the Southern Rockies/Central and Southern Plains into the Mid-Mississippi and Tennessee Valley on August 19th, with compressional warming beneath the ridge contributing to extensive warming across much of North Louisiana, Southern Arkansas, and portions of extreme Eastern Texas. Cloud cover leftover from decayed scattered showers and thunderstorms that developed across the area on the 18th also limited the extent of cooling during the overnight/early morning hours into the 19th, with temperatures only falling to near 80 degrees. This provided a head start to strong diurnal heating during the day, with afternoon temperatures climbing to well in excess of 100 degrees over these areas. An upper level ridge of high pressure was centered over much of Texas on August 8th-9th, with increased subsidence beneath the ridge allowing temperatures across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, extreme Southwest Arkansas, and Northwest Louisiana to climb into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees. A light southerly wind on the backside of surface high pressure over the Lower Mississippi Valley maintained ample low level moisture and limited the extent of mixing, resulting in heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees across the aforementioned areas.

An upper level ridge of high pressure built back over the Lower Mississippi Valley into the Four State Region during the final couple of days of July, resulting in more widespread upper 90s to triple digit temperatures across portions of extreme Eastern Texas. Unfortunately, dewpoints were not able to mix out much during the afternoons of July 30th-31st, with oppressively hot conditions leading to resultant heat indices ranging from 110-115 degrees each day across portions of extreme Eastern Texas.

An upper level ridge of high pressure over the Southeast United States began to retrograde west across the Lower Mississippi Valley into the Four State Region during the final several days of July, resulting in the return of much hotter temperatures as they climbed back into the mid 90s to near 100 degrees. While dewpoints were able to mix out to some extent, resultant heat indices still ranged from 105 to 110 degrees from the 27th through the 29th across portions of extreme Eastern Texas. However, more widespread triple digit temperatures were observed on the 30th and 31st, and dewpoints were unable to mix out much through these days, resulting in more oppressively hot conditions with heat indices ranging from 110-115 degrees to end July.

Following the passage of a westward moving tropical wave on July 19th across North Louisiana and East Texas, upper ridging expanded back west into much of the Four State Region from the Southeast Gulf Coast on the 20th, and persisted through the 25th. Strong subsidence beneath the ridge resulted in additional compressional warming, which enabled afternoon temperatures to climb into the mid and upper 90s across Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, extreme Eastern Texas and North Louisiana. Coupled with ample low level moisture that persisted across the area, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees each day.

recent.narrative: A large but strong upper level ridge of high pressure expanded from the Southern Rockies/Central and Southern Plains into the Mid-Mississippi Valley on August 14th, with compressional warming beneath the ridge contributing to extensive warming across much of Southwest Arkansas, Southeast Oklahoma, and East Texas. Sinking air beneath the ridge and strong insolation allowed for afternoon temperatures to climb into the upper 90s to near 100 degrees over these areas. When combined with the high humidity, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees across much of Southwest Arkansas, Southeast Oklahoma, and East Texas, which persisted through the 20th.

An upper level ridge of high pressure was centered over much of Texas on August 8th-9th, with increased subsidence beneath the ridge allowing temperatures across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, extreme Southwest Arkansas, and Northwest Louisiana to climb into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees. Compressional warming ahead of the front resulted in temperatures climbing into the mid and upper 90s across Lower East Texas and North Louisiana along and south of Interstate 20. Low level moisture pooling along the frontal zone did not allow for much mixing of the dewpoints during the afternoon, which when combined with these temperatures, resulted in heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees.

While dewpoints were able to mix out to some extent, resultant heat indices still ranged from 105 to 110 degrees from the 27th through the 31st across much of East Texas before showers and thunderstorms that developed during the afternoon of the 31st significantly cooled temperatures late in the day.

Coupled with ample low level moisture that spread back west into the area from Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana ahead of another westerly moving tropical wave across the Northern Gulf, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees on the 24th and 25th.

A maximum wind gust of 66 MPH was observed at the West Texas Mesonet site, 3WNW Fluvanna.
A maximum wind gust of 64 MPH was observed at the West Texas Mesonet site, 2ESE Gail.
A maximum wind gust of 67 MPH was observed at the West Texas Mesonet site, 3WNW Fluvanna.
A maximum wind gust of 61 MPH was reported at the RAWS station, FRKT2 Gail.
A maximum wind gust of 63 MPH was observed at the West Texas Mesonet Station, 2SE Gail.
Several trees were down and a large carport of a home was collapsed in Wills Point.
Video on X showed several trees blown down in Canton. News reports indicated several homes and businesses suffered roof damage and booths at Canton Trade Days were also damaged.

An EF-0 tornado touched down around 9.5 miles east of Canton along CR 1321 then moved northeast passing south and east of Grand Saline before crossing US Highway 80 and lifting north of Silver Lake. One home on FM 1255 lost part of the wall on an addition built over the garage, and a mobile home along FM 1255 near CR 1605 had roof and porch damage. Another home suffered roof damage on CR 1701. Several trees were also uprooted or damaged along the path. The tornado may have crossed into Wood County for a short distance, but due to the lack of roads in the area this could not be confirmed. Maximum estimated winds were 80 mph.

A member of the public reported damage to his property. A shed with metal siding and a wooden frame was destroyed, with pieces of wood thrown several hundred years. Posts cemented 8-10 ft in the ground were pulled up with the cement. A 20 by 20 equipment shed was moved and angled around 45 degrees.
Broadcast media reported a collapsed metal multi-vehicle shed.

Social media pictures showed damaged wooden/metal buildings (side of one collapsed, the other partially collapsed and lifted off of its foundation), a bent metal tower, and a wooden structure housing tractors destroyed.

costliest.narrative: Notable flooding was reported around Canton. Specifically: Streets and roads were flooded along Rollins Rd and water may have entered a few homes. The EM's office on SH 64 experienced flooding around the office, and water up to 5 deep entered the office. Outside the office, pictures show the water was at least a foot deep in some areas. The location of First Trade Days was flooded with over a foot of water in some areas.
Amateur radio reported water covering Highway 80 through Grand Saline, with some downtown businesses also flooded.
A shoe store building collapsed at 4th St and High St in Wills Point.

Trained spotter reported trees 12-24 inches in diameter uprooted/split between I-20 and HWY-64 just north of Canton. Widespread trees knocked down were reported across the county. An upper level system coincided with abundant atmospheric moisture across the Texas Panhandle on the evening of the 24th. This resulted in scattered thunderstorms that eventually grew into widespread thunderstorm activity. A few storms became strong to severe thunderstorms that produced heavy rainfall, severe wind gusts, and a localized occurrence of hail up to ping pong ball size. The biggest hazard that occurred during this event was the flash flooding that occurred in the Amarillo and Canyon areas. The widespread thunderstorms produced very heavy rainfall and storms continued to move over the same locations. Flash flooding resulted in stalled cars and flooded and closed roadways. Flooding in Palo Duro Canyon State Park resulted in flooded roads and a few of the campsites had to be evacuated.

During the overnight to early morning hours of July 7th, a small upper level system helped produce a cluster of strong to severe storms straddling the Texas-Oklahoma state line. A power pole and several large tree branches were snapped in Wheeler, TX as a result, with another severe gust occurring further south in Clarendon. While this was ongoing, another line of storms entered the Oklahoma Panhandle from Kansas, generating a 64 mph wind gust in Hooker, OK.
Quarter to golfball size hail fell on the north side of Howardwick.

During the afternoon of the 26th several isolated supercells formed in the eastern Texas Panhandle and some produced hail up to the size of tennis balls. After these storms moved east of the Panhandle, a storm complex moved into the southwestern Texas Panhandle from New Mexico. costliest.narrative: A tornado touched down on the southwest side of Clarendon, continuing through Greenbelt Reservoir before dissipating northeast of Howardwick. Minor damage to homes and Clarendon College was observed on the west side of Clarendon. The tornado took on a wider path and strengthened as it progressed toward Greenbelt Reservoir causing considerable damage to mobile homes, recreational vehicles, and boating facilities. In addition, several power poles of varying sizes were downed and many trees were snapped in the area.

This tornado touched down after the initial parent tornado occluded. Based on spotter/chaser video, it appears to have developed in about the same locations as the first Clarendon tornado. It became wide, likely going over the same locations as the previous tornado. It then started to follow the rim of the mesocyclone, likely being more of a satellite tornado around the main mesocyclone. The tornado was recorded as being on the ground for about 15 minutes before finally lifting. It likely did not move very fast before finally becoming corkscrew in nature before lifting. Damage seems to be limited to mesquite brush damage. However, the worst known damage was to a water pumping windmill which was toppled and destroyed by the tornado. The maximum estimated winds were 90mph.
A collapsing thunderstorm brought damaging winds to locations northeast of Howardwick. Irrigation pivots were blown over and a barn was damaged. Tree branches were also snapped and torn off of trees.

A very potent upper level system produced widespread hazards from heavy snow across the front range/Rockies to severe weather across the Southern High Plains. The vigorous closed upper low was approached the Four Corners region from the west. A warm front lifted north and northwest across all but the Oklahoma Panhandle and the northwest Texas Panhandle while a sharpening dryline was located over eastern New Mexico. The dryline preceded a Pacific cold front which was also located in eastern New Mexico and swept eastward later in the evening. A broken line of thunderstorms developed ahead of the dryline in eastern New Mexico and tracked north and east into the western and southwestern Texas Panhandle before continuing to move east across the remainder of the eastern Panhandles during the evening hours, growing upscale as the Pacific cold front swept eastward and overtook the dryline. An upper level weather disturbance moved across the region late in the evening on August 2nd through the early morning hours of August 3rd. This, combined with sufficient instability and wind shear, brought severe thunderstorms to the combined Panhandles. These storms moved in from Kansas and brought hail and damaging winds to the region. The most significant of the severe storms moved through portions of the north central Texas Panhandle, where radar estimates and associated damage from straight line winds were estimated to have reached 90 to 100mph in portions of Moore and Hutchinson counties.

During the evening of July 10th, isolated storms produced significant downburst winds in the northwest Oklahoma Panhandle. As an upper level disturbance interacted with sufficient atmospheric wind and dry air, storms were able to produce strong winds potentially up to 80mph. This resulted in significant damage in portions of Cimarron County. Later into the overnight hours, as storms were diminishing, there were some severe wind gusts related to a potential heat burst.

The peak downburst wind gust of 60 mph occurred at 1821CDT with 2 additional gusts of 58 mph shortly after.

A large but strong upper level ridge of high pressure expanded from the Southern Rockies/Central and Southern Plains into the Mid-Mississippi Valley on August 14th, with compressional warming beneath the ridge contributing to extensive warming across much of Southwest Arkansas, Southeast Oklahoma, and East Texas. Sinking air beneath the ridge and strong insolation allowed for afternoon temperatures to climb into the upper 90s to near 100 degrees over these areas. When combined with the high humidity, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees across much of Southwest Arkansas, Southeast Oklahoma, and East Texas, which persisted through the 20th.

An upper level ridge of high pressure was centered over much of Texas on August 8th-9th, with increased subsidence beneath the ridge allowing temperatures across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, extreme Southwest Arkansas, and Northwest Louisiana to climb into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees. A light southerly wind on the backside of surface high pressure over the Lower Mississippi Valley maintained ample low level moisture and limited the extent of mixing, resulting in heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees across the aforementioned areas.

An upper level ridge of high pressure over the Southeast United States began to retrograde west across the Lower Mississippi Valley into the Four State Region during the final several days of July, resulting in the return of much hotter temperatures as they climbed back into the mid 90s to near 100 degrees. While dewpoints were able to mix out to some extent, resultant heat indices still ranged from 105 to 110 degrees from the 27th through the 31st across much of East Texas before showers and thunderstorms that developed during the afternoon of the 31st significantly cooled temperatures late in the day.

Following multiple days of persistent upper ridging over much of the Four State Region from July 20th-24th, strong subsidence beneath the ridge resulted in additional compressional warming, which enabled afternoon temperatures to climb into the mid 90s across the western sections of East Texas. Coupled with ample low level moisture that spread back west into the area from Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana ahead of another westerly moving tropical wave across the Northern Gulf, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees on the 24th and 25th.

A strong upper-level high pressure ridge expanded and intensified across the South Central and Southeast portions of the U.S. late in the month of June and persisted for several days. Increasing southerly flow in response to the eastward advancing high pressure ridge allowed rich Gulf moisture and elevated humidity levels to combine with daily high temperatures in the lower to middle 90s across all of East and Northeast Texas, resulting in peak heat index values between 105-109 degrees each day from June 20th through June 24th.

Areas of rain developed across much of the Four State Region during the afternoon hours of February 18th through the early morning hours of the 19th, along and behind an arctic cold front that moved into the region ahead of a strong upper trough of low pressure that translated east across the Southern Plains and Ozarks. While the precipitation ended across Northeast Texas before temperatures fell to or below freezing, areas of standing water quickly froze with the arrival of the subfreezing temperatures during the early morning hours of the 19th, with portions of this area observing a thin coat of ice on area roadways. A late spring cold front pushed south into the area on Monday June 12, and became stationary near the I-20 corridor. The front provided focus for thunderstorm development as it meandered across the region for most of that weak, with multiple upper level disturbances providing added lift for development. Several consecutive days of strong to severe storms was the result, with many areas receiving large hail (storms each day produced hail over 2) and some locations receiving damaging downburst winds between 75-95 mph. Severe storms produced hail up to tennis ball sized, and parts of Central Texas experienced winds of 70-80 mph. Additionally, part of the awning and roof of Rigo's Tire Shop and Road Service was torn off and tossed approximately 100 feet down the road. Radar velocity from the Corpus Christi radar indicated winds of 58 knots about 4,000 feet in elevation between 7:15PM CDT and 7:20PM CDT, which was used to estimate the timing of the event.

recent.narrative: Extreme (D3) Drought developed across the the northern third of the Kenedy County portion of Padre Island National Seashore (PINS), on November 18th and continued through and beyond month's end.  The combination of dryness, warm to hot temperatures, and very low soil moisture contributed to the worsening condition here.

Severe (D2) level drought expanded to cover the northern two-thirds of Kenedy County's barrier island (Padre Island National Seashore) on March 25th, courtesy of breezy to windy, generally dry (low humidity) days, and above average day/night temperatures with no wetting dew.  Conditions would improve soon after rains on March 27-28, but the improvements were not recognized until the April 1st Drought Monitor update.||Unknown was impact to livestock (mainly cattle) in these areas.

Sarita Texas Water Development Board mesonet station recorded 12 hours, from 11:15pm on February 19 to 11:15am on February 20, of freezing temperatures (temperatures at or below 32F degrees).  By proxy, as well as from observations along the coast at Baffin Bay and Rincon del San Jose, similar conditions extended all the way to the Kenedy County barrier island.

The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON)/C-MAN platform at Brazos Santiago (South Padre Island), along the Isla Blanca jetty just inshore from the beachfront, recorded a prolonged period of much higher than predicted tides, with departures generally 2 feet or more above predicted through the period.  Astronomical tides were generally low, and this likely reduced the potential for property damage beyond severe and extensive beach erosion.  The time period selected combined the above predicted tides with long-period swells and high waves, each which increased both run-up and wave set-up to cause erosion, which peaked at high tide but also occurred between high and low tide cycles.||An unknown amount of dune calving likely occurred along Padre Island National Seashore (PINS) along the Kenedy County coastline at narrower beaches.  There were no known new cuts from the water levels

Harlingen ASOS recorded 33 hours of wind chills at or below 30F degrees from 11:30pm on January 20 to 9:45am on January 22, 2025. This includes 7 hours of wind chills at or below 20F degrees from 3:52am to 11:05 am on January 21, and 9.5 hours of the same from 10:30pm on January 21 to 7:52am on January 22. A minimum wind chill temperature of 17-18F degrees occurred between 3:52am to 7:52am on January 21, and again from 4:52am to 6:52am on January 22.  By proxy and interpolation, similar values were likely across much of coastal Willacy County during the same period, as northwest flow drove the cold air (and low wind chills) to Port Mansfield, along the west shore of Laguna Madre Bay.

The Cameron County Airport near Bayview recorded an estimated 5 hours of heat index between 111F and 114F.  By proxy, and accounting for slightly lower temperatures and heat index in inland Kenedy County, the likely time of dangerous heat (111F to 115F) was one hour less on each side of the observation from Bayview, for coastal Willacy County.

The Cameron County Airport Automated Surface Observing Sensor near Bayview recorded around 4.5 hours of heat index values between 111 and 115F between 1153 AM CDT and 430 PM CDT. Peak values of 115 occurred between 253 and 353 PM.  By proxy, it can be interpolated that Coastal Willacy also observed similar heat index values during the same time.

Rincon del San Jose in Coastal Kenedy County recorded temperatures at or below freezing for 5.5 hours (between 330 AM and 9 AM on the 17th). A minimum temperature of 29F was recorded at 8 AM on the 17th.  By proxy, and based on interpolation of temperatures from northeast coastal Cameron County, a shorter duration of freezing temperatures was likely, with minimum temperatures estimated to be around 30 degrees F.

A Minimum Wind Chill value of 11F and 13F degrees was recorded in Bayview and Realitos at 6:55 AM and 7:54 AM, respectively. By proxy, it is assumed that similar conditions occurred in coastal Willacy County, including Port Mansfield. The duration of temperatures within the wind chill criteria was anywhere between 10-12 hours.

costliest.narrative: High northeasterly winds, associated with a wake low developing behind a thunderstorm complex, contributed to enhanced northeasterly swell which led to coastal flooding across portions of Coastal Willacy County on the afternoon of April 23rd. Water levels topped out at 2.38ft above mean sea level (an estimated for water levels above normally dry ground) around 2:12PM CDT in the Port Mansfield area. Pictures from the Emergency Manager in Port Mansfield shows portions of docks damaged or washed away.

recent.narrative: A closed upper low over the Texas Panhandle with a potent jet stream rounding its base led to widespread westerly high winds across much of southeast New Mexico and west Texas.

This is a continuation of the previous day's event. A large, positively-tilted trough over the western US with a leading jet streak resulted in a prolonged and widespread period of high winds across much of southeast New Mexico and west Texas. Wind damage was reported in some locations due to this high-end synoptic wind event.

A deep and broad upper-level trough was located across the western US. A very strong jet stream with numerous embedded shortwaves resulted in westerly strong and high winds across much of the region. Intense high winds were reported across the higher elevations with high winds and blowing dust across a large portion of the plains.
A maximum wind gust of 60 MPH was observed at the CWOP site, FW9691 Mentone.

This event consisted of a highly amplified weather pattern with an ejecting closed upper-low moving into the southern Rocky Mountains. This system and accompanying jet brought a high-end wind event to southeast New Mexico and much of west Texas. High winds and property damage were reported across a large portion of the area. Additionally, blowing dust greatly reduced visibility at times.
There was a report from a trained spotter of baseball size hail at the intersection of FM2687 and FM649.
Emergency Management reported a tree on a car in Hebbronville. Wind speed estimated.

A complex of showers and storms moved through Jim Hogg County the evening of September 15th into the very early morning hours of September 16th. According to utility companies, over half of their customers lost power during the event. Unfortunately, this led to the AWOS in Hebbronville to stop reporting shortly before the worst of the storm arrived. Before it went offline, the AWOS station recorded a gust of 38 mph. The combination of the number of power outages coupled with radar data was used a guide for this event.
The Hebbronville RAWS site recorded a wind gust of 54 knots at 9:46PM CDT.

Member of the public shared a picture of a hail stone that was estimated to be about the size of a quarter in the Hebbronville area at 9:10AM CDT. The post was made at 9:14AM CDT and radar corroborated the report.

Nickel to quarter sized hail was reported by the public around 9:25PM CDT a little over 2 miles southwest of Hebbronville along Texas Highway 16 near the intersection of Farm to Market 3073. Additional reports of penny to quarter sized hail were reported by the public from the same storm in and around the town of Hebbronville between 9:30PM CDT and 9:50PM CDT.

recent.narrative: Light snow began during the early morning hours across upper Jefferson County with heavy snow moving in around sunrise. Accumulations ranged from 3 to 6 inches.

A prolonged drought that began earlier in the year peaked during the first week of November. Thunderstorms returned to upper Jefferson County by the 10th with more regular rains following after that date. Forest areas and crawfish suffered considerable die offs plus rice, soybeans, and hay yields were reduced, but specific dollar estimates are unknown at this time.

The average temperature at Beaumont during the month of August was 89.2F which broke the old record of 87.7F set in 2011. The hottest temperature during the month was 111F on the 27th which broke the all time high record of 108F which was hit most recently as August 24, 2023. Beaumont also experienced the 4th driest August ever recorded. Jefferson County and deep Southeast Texas was under an excessive heat warning for 15 days of the month and only went without any heat products for 4 days of the month.
